A close reading for the week

“Was this the face…?”

Doctor Faustus · the Helen speech

Days from damnation, Faustus asks the spirits to bring him Helen of Troy. What he says to her is the most famous praise of beauty in English drama, and every image in it is on fire.

FAUSTUSWas this the face that launch’d a thousand ships,1
And burnt the topless towers of Ilium2—

  1. 1

    Praise that counts the dead

    The most famous compliment in English drama measures beauty in warships. A thousand ships means a decade of siege and slaughter: Helen’s face is praised by the size of the catastrophe it caused. And it opens as a question (“Was this the face?”), as if Faustus, the scholar to the last, needs the legend verified before he commits to it.

  2. 2

    Towers without tops

    “Topless” means so high their tops cannot be seen, and those measureless towers exist in the line only as burning. Ilium is Troy. From its first image the speech can only praise by destroying: the city stands in the verse for the length of one word before the fire takes it.
